common_name: Bar Harbor Juniper (Dense Plum-Winter Coastal Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Bar Harbor tolerates coastal salt spray and dry, sandy soil better than most groundcover junipers, but will not tolerate standing water.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Bar Harbor was selected on the coast of Maine and is notably salt- and wind-tolerant, making it a favorite for seaside banks and dune stabilization as well as inland dry slopes. The trailing stems form a dense, tight mat of fine, gray-green to blue-green foliage that presses close to the ground, denser and lower than many other creeping juniper selections, and the foliage shifts to a distinctive plum-purple cast through the cold months before greening up again in spring. Its tight, weed-suppressing habit suits rock gardens, retaining-wall cascades, and erosion control on dry, sunny banks. Water during the first season to establish, then rely on rainfall, and avoid overhead irrigation that keeps the dense mat wet, which invites fungal blight.

common_name: Prince of Wales Juniper (Bright Green Low Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Prince of Wales is a Canadian-selected creeping juniper valued for holding bright green color through winter rather than shifting to purple or bronze tones.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Prince of Wales tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and declines quickly in wet, poorly drained ground. Selected in Alberta, this creeping juniper hugs the ground in a very low, trailing mat rarely more than a few inches tall, with fine-textured, bright green foliage that keeps its clean green color through winter rather than turning purple or bronze like many other creeping juniper cultivars. Its flat, dense habit makes it a reliable choice for covering dry sunny banks, cascading over walls, and filling gaps between stepping stones or larger shrubs in a low-water landscape. Water during the establishment year, then rely mainly on rainfall, and avoid wetting the dense foliage late in the day to reduce the risk of fungal blight.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Pfitzer juniper is one of the most widely planted landscape conifers in North America and tolerates heat, drought, and poor alkaline soil once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Pfitzer juniper will not tolerate soggy or heavy clay ground and needs sharp drainage to avoid root rot. A hybrid between Juniperus chinensis and J. sabina first raised in Germany in the early 1900s, it forms a large, wide-spreading, irregularly vase-shaped mound of soft, feathery, gray-green foliage on branches that angle upward and outward from the base, giving it a coarser, more informal texture than the tighter, more upright chinensis cultivars. Its bulk and rapid establishment make it a classic choice for large-scale screening, bank stabilization, and filling wide foundation corners where a big, low-maintenance evergreen mass is wanted, though its eventual size means it needs generous room to avoid constant shearing. Prune only to remove wayward branches and improve air circulation, since heavy shearing spoils its naturally billowing form and stresses the plant in humid climates prone to juniper blight.

common_name: Kaizuka Juniper (Hollywood Juniper, Twisted-Branch Sculptural Conifer)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; Kaizuka is very heat- and drought-tolerant once established but benefits from occasional pruning to open up its dense, twisting branch structure and improve air circulation.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; Kaizuka will not tolerate wet, heavy clay and needs sharp drainage to avoid root and canker disease. Widely sold in the trade as Hollywood juniper, this irregular, sculptural cultivar produces thick, twisting, cloud-like tufts of rich green, cord-like foliage on branches that curve and contort as the plant matures, creating a bold, living-sculpture silhouette unlike the tidy cones or flat mats of most other juniper cultivars. Its dramatic, asymmetrical form makes it a striking specimen or accent planting where a single strong architectural statement is wanted, and it takes well to selective pruning to accentuate its natural twisting habit, in the style of Japanese garden design. It tolerates heat, wind, and coastal conditions well but is prone to juniper twig blight and spider mites in humid, poorly ventilated sites, so give it full sun and open air circulation.

common_name: Old Gold Juniper (Compact Golden Mounding Conifer)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Old Gold holds its gold color best in full sun and tends to green up in shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Old Gold will not tolerate soggy or heavy clay soil and needs sharp drainage to avoid root and crown rot. A compact sport of the popular Pfitzer group, Old Gold forms a low, broad, irregularly mounding shrub with dense, feathery sprays of rich golden-yellow foliage that holds its color through the year better in sun than in shade, more compact and slower-growing than the larger green and blue Pfitzer-type junipers. Its bright, low mounding form makes it a useful color accent for foundation plantings, mixed shrub borders, and large rock gardens where a smaller-scale gold conifer is wanted. Prune only to remove wayward branches, since its naturally tidy mounded habit needs little shaping, and give it full sun and good air circulation to reduce the risk of fungal blight common to junipers in humid climates.

common_name: Blue Carpet Juniper (Vigorous Spreading Silvery-Blue Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; like other junipers, Blue Carpet will not tolerate wet feet and needs sharp drainage.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Carpet will not tolerate soggy or heavy clay soil and needs sharp drainage to avoid root and crown rot. This vigorous, wide-spreading Dutch-raised selection sends out long, arching branches clothed in dense, prickly, intensely silvery-blue foliage, growing considerably faster and wider than the slow, mounding Blue Star, making it far better suited to covering large sunny banks or slopes than filling a small rock-garden niche. Its rapid spread and strong blue color make it an effective large-scale groundcover for erosion control and mass plantings where quick coverage is wanted. It needs little to no pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward branch, is extremely drought-tolerant once established, and holds its blue color year-round in most climates.

common_name: Apollo Mahonia (Low Spreading Heavy-Flowering Oregon Grape)

planting.note: Plant container stock or bare-root plants in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade, tolerating more sun than most mahonias in cooler climates; Apollo is a low, spreading Dutch selection of Oregon grape bred for unusually heavy flowering.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade, avoiding exposed sites with harsh winter wind and afternoon sun; Apollo is a low, dense, spreading selection of the Pacific Northwest native Oregon grape, staying under 2 feet tall while slowly forming a broad colony by suckering. It is prized for an unusually profuse spring flower display — dense clusters of brilliant yellow flowers smother the branch tips in early spring, noticeably heavier than the species — followed by the same dusty-blue, tart, edible berries and spiny, holly-like evergreen foliage that turns bronze-purple in cold weather. Its low, spreading habit and heavy bloom make Apollo a strong choice for a flowering groundcover under high shade or as a foreground planting in a shaded shrub border. Prune only to remove dead or leggy canes at ground level, since its naturally low, suckering habit needs little other maintenance.
